q: What is MLOps?
o: A tool that trains models without any code
A cloud provider for GPUs
A type of neural network
The practices for building, deploying, monitoring and updating machine learning systems reliably
e:
MLOps brings DevOps ideas (automation, testing, versioning, monitoring) to machine learning.
It exists because an ML system is more than a model: it also depends on data, code and the environment, and all of them change over time.
The goal is to move from a notebook that works once to a service that keeps working.
r: MLOps = running ML in production reliably.

q: Why is a trained model not the end of an ML project?
o: Because training results are random and cannot be trusted
Because real-world data changes, so the model must be deployed, monitored and updated
Because models stop working after a fixed number of days
Because a model cannot be saved to a file
e:
A model is trained on a snapshot of the past. Customers, prices, sensors and fraud patterns keep changing, so its quality can fall without any code change.
Shipping it is the start of the work: serving, watching it and retraining when needed.
No model has a built-in expiry date; it is the data around it that moves.
r: The world changes, so the model needs care after launch.

q: What does "serving" a model mean?
o: Training it on more data
Storing the training dataset
Making the trained model available so that other systems can send it data and get predictions
Printing its metrics
e:
Serving is the step that puts a model to work. It can be a web API that answers each request, a job that scores a table overnight, or code inside an app or device.
The serving side has its own concerns: latency, throughput, availability, cost and versions.
Training and serving are separate stages and often run on different machines.
r: Serving = putting the model where it can make predictions.

q: A shop e-mails each customer a list of recommended products every night. Which kind of inference fits best?
o: Batch prediction: score all customers in one scheduled job
Online (real-time) prediction through an API for every e-mail
Prediction on the customer's phone
Retraining the model for every customer
e:
Nobody is waiting for the answer while it is computed, and the inputs are known in advance. A scheduled batch job is simpler and cheaper than keeping a real-time service running.
Online inference is for when a user or a system needs the prediction within milliseconds or seconds, for example during a payment.
Batch results are then stored and read when needed.
r: No one waiting: batch. Someone waiting: online.

q: Why do teams version their models and datasets, not only their code?
o: Because Python requires it
To make training faster
To reproduce a result, compare versions and roll back, by knowing exactly which data and code produced each model
To make files smaller
e:
A model is the product of code, data, parameters and environment. If you only version the code, you cannot rebuild the model, because the data may have changed.
With versions you can answer "what is running in production?" and "what changed since last month?", and go back if the new one is worse.
Tools range from Git plus data versioning tools to a model registry.
r: Version data and models to reproduce and roll back.

q: What is a model registry?
o: A list of the hyperparameters of one model
A log of all prediction requests
A cloud bucket for raw datasets
A catalogue of model versions with their metadata (metrics, data and code used, stage), so you know what is approved and what is deployed
e:
The registry is the shared record of the models a team has built. Each entry points to the model files and says which run created it, how it scored and whether it is in staging or production.
It lets deployment tools fetch "the approved version" instead of a file someone copied by hand.
It usually supports stages or aliases and an audit trail of who promoted what.
r: Registry = versions + metadata + stage.

q: Only one person can rebuild the production model, by running a long notebook by hand in the right order. What is the main fix?
o: Add comments to the notebook
Turn the steps (load data, validate, train, evaluate, register) into an automated, versioned pipeline that anyone can run
Ask the person to stay in the team
Retrain the model less often
e:
Manual notebooks hide knowledge in one person's memory and cannot be scheduled, tested or audited.
A pipeline makes each step a defined, repeatable unit with explicit inputs and outputs, so a run can be triggered by a schedule, by new data or by a code change.
Notebooks are still fine for exploration; the pipeline is for what goes to production.
r: Automate the steps in a pipeline.

q: Which signal of data drift can you monitor in production even before any labels arrive?
o: A comparison of the distribution of live inputs with the training data, for example with a PSI or KS statistic
The training loss of the model
The size of the model file
The number of hyperparameters
e:
Drift means the data the model sees now differs from what it learned from. You can measure that on the inputs alone, because inputs need no labels.
Common checks compare each feature's live distribution with a reference window using statistics such as the Population Stability Index (PSI) or the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test.
It is an early warning: drift does not always lower quality, and quality can drop without input drift.
r: Compare live inputs with the training reference.

q: How can you release a new model version with low risk?
o: Replace the old model for everyone at once, at night
Send a small share of real traffic to the new version (a canary), compare its metrics with the old one, and increase the share step by step
Test it only offline and then deploy
Give it to the internal team forever
e:
A canary exposes only a few users to a possible problem, while real traffic shows how the model behaves with real data and real load.
If the error rate, latency or business metrics are worse, you stop and send the traffic back. If they are fine, you ramp up.
Offline tests cannot show everything that happens in production.
r: Canary: small share first, then ramp up.

q: What is a shadow deployment of a model?
o: A model trained on data from other companies
A copy of the model in another region
A model that only runs at night
The new model receives copies of real requests and its predictions are logged and compared, but users never see them
e:
Shadow mode tests a model on real inputs with zero user impact. You can compare its predictions and latency with the live model.
Its limit: it gives no evidence on how users react, because they never see its output. For that you need a canary or an A/B test.
It does double the compute for the shadowed traffic.
r: Shadow = real traffic, no user impact.

q: A new model version is live and the error rate and latency of the service jumped. What is the fastest safe action?
o: Roll back to the previous model version, then investigate
Debug it while it keeps serving everyone
Retrain the new model right away
Add more traffic to see if it improves
e:
Reduce the damage first, then find the cause. A rollback is only quick if the previous version is still available and deployable, which is a reason to keep versions in a registry.
Investigation then happens offline or in staging, with logs and sample requests from the incident.
Good practice: decide the rollback rule before the release.
r: Roll back first, investigate after.

q: What should experiment tracking record for each training run?
o: Only the best metric
Only the final model file
The code version, data version, parameters, metrics, environment and output artifacts
A screenshot of the notebook
e:
To compare runs and to repeat one later you need everything that influenced it: code commit, data snapshot, hyperparameters, library versions and random seed, plus the results and the files produced.
Tools such as MLflow store these in a searchable list, so "which run gave 0.91 and how?" has an answer.
A single metric without its context cannot be reproduced.
r: Track code, data, parameters, metrics and artifacts.

q: Why is a model usually packaged in a container for serving?
o: It makes the model more accurate
It makes training faster
It removes the need for monitoring
The dependencies and versions are the same in development, testing and production, so it behaves the same everywhere
e:
"It worked on my laptop" is common in ML because of the many libraries involved and their versions. A container image bundles the code, the model and the exact dependencies.
The same image is promoted from test to production and can be scaled by an orchestrator.
It does not change the accuracy: it makes the environment predictable.
r: Container = same environment everywhere.

q: A model server groups several incoming requests into one batch before running the model on a GPU. What is the trade-off?
o: Higher throughput and better hardware use, at the cost of some extra waiting time (latency) for each request
Higher accuracy for lower throughput
Lower cost and lower latency at the same time, always
No trade-off: it only changes the logs
e:
GPUs are most efficient when they process many inputs at once. Waiting a few milliseconds to fill a batch raises the number of requests handled per second.
But the first request in a batch waits for the others, so its latency grows. Dynamic batching lets you cap that wait.
Tune the maximum batch size and wait time against your latency target.
r: Batching: more throughput, a bit more latency.

q: What problem does a feature store mainly solve?
o: It stores the trained models
It gives one shared, versioned definition of each feature for both training and serving, avoiding duplicated code and mismatches
It makes the GPU faster
It replaces the data warehouse
e:
Without a shared definition, the data team computes a feature in SQL for training and the engineers rewrite it in code for production, and the two drift apart (training-serving skew).
A feature store computes or serves the feature from one definition, offers an offline store for training and an online store for low-latency lookups, and lets teams reuse features.
It does not train models or replace the warehouse; it sits between the data and the models.
r: Feature store = one feature definition for training and serving.

q: A model service returns HTTP 200 for every request, but a bug makes it predict almost the same value for everyone. Which monitoring would catch this?
o: Uptime and HTTP status codes
CPU usage graphs
Monitoring of the distribution of predictions and of the inputs, not only service health
The size of the log files
e:
Normal service monitoring (uptime, errors, latency, CPU) says the system is healthy. The prediction here is wrong, not the service.
ML monitoring adds the data: the distribution of inputs, the distribution of predictions (a sudden constant or a shifted mean is a warning), and quality metrics when labels arrive.
Both layers are needed.
r: Watch the data and predictions, not only the service.

q: Which is a sensible way to decide when to retrain a model?
o: Every time any library has a new version
Whenever a developer feels like it
On a schedule that fits how fast the data changes, plus triggers from monitoring such as drift or a quality drop
Never: a good model does not need updates
e:
Retraining costs compute and carries risk, so it should be a decision based on evidence, not on habit.
Start with a schedule that matches the pace of change (daily for ads, monthly for a stable process), and add triggers: drift alerts, a drop in quality once labels arrive, or new data volume.
Every retrained model still goes through the same evaluation gate before replacing the current one.
r: Retrain by schedule plus evidence from monitoring.

q: What are the stages of a production ML pipeline?
a:
- Ingest: pull the data from its sources, with a fixed snapshot or time range.
- Validate: check schema, nulls, ranges and distributions; stop if the data is bad.
- Prepare: compute the features with the same code used for serving.
- Train and tune: run with tracked code, data version, parameters and seed.
- Evaluate: compare with a baseline and the current model on a fixed holdout, including key slices.
- Register: store the model with its metadata and lineage in the registry.
- Deploy and monitor: release gradually, watch the service, inputs, predictions and quality, and retrain or roll back when needed.

q: To build a training set, each row is joined to the latest value of a feature `customer_total_spend`, taken from a table that is updated daily. The model is great offline and poor online. What is the likely problem?
o: The table is too small
The join used values from after the event time, a leak; features must be joined as they were at that moment (a point-in-time join)
The model is too simple
The table needs more indexes
e:
For a row dated 1 March, the feature must be the value known on 1 March. Using the latest value includes purchases made after that date, so the model sees the future in training, but not in production.
A point-in-time (as-of) join picks, for each row, the latest feature value with a timestamp not after the row's event time.
Feature stores such as Feast do this correctly.
r: Join features as they were at event time.

q: How can you check systematically for training-serving skew in a live system?
o: Compare the training loss with the validation loss
Check the Docker image size
Increase the number of replicas
Log the exact features the model receives in production and compare them with the same features recomputed offline, or with the training distributions
e:
Skew means the model gets different inputs in production than the pipeline gave it in training. The way to see it is to look at what it really receives.
Logging serving features (sampled) lets you compare them with an offline recomputation for the same requests, which finds code differences, or with training statistics, which finds missing values, changed units or encodings.
The best prevention is to run the same feature code in both places.
r: Log serving features and compare them with offline values.

q: With millions of rows per day, a statistical drift test flags almost every feature as "significantly different" every day, with tiny p-values. What is a better approach?
o: Use the size of the change (for example a distance or PSI) with thresholds tied to its impact, instead of p-values alone
Ignore drift monitoring altogether
Lower the p-value threshold to 0.5
Retrain automatically each time a test fails
e:
With huge samples, even a harmless difference becomes statistically significant, so the alert never stops and gets ignored.
A drift measure with a magnitude (PSI, Jensen-Shannon distance, Wasserstein distance) lets you set thresholds on how big a change matters, and you can prioritize the features the model relies on most.
Always confirm that an alert corresponds to a real effect on predictions or quality.
r: Alert on the size of the change, not only significance.

q: You need real evidence that a new recommender raises purchases. Which rollout gives it?
o: An A/B test with random assignment of users to the old and the new model
A shadow deployment
An offline test on last year's data
Asking colleagues which one looks better
e:
Random assignment makes the two groups comparable, so a difference in purchases can be attributed to the model.
Shadow mode logs predictions but users never see them, so it says nothing about behaviour. Offline data reflects the old system's choices.
Decide the metric and the sample size before the test starts, and run it for full weekly cycles.
r: A/B test = causal evidence of user impact.

q: The training pipeline runs in CI with the same code and data as last month, but the metrics changed. What do you check first?
o: The color of the dashboard
The number of CPU cores
Unpinned library versions, random seeds and whether the data snapshot is really the same
The name of the branch
e:
Reproducibility needs all the inputs fixed: exact dependency versions (a lock file), random seeds, the data snapshot (not "the latest table") and the configuration.
A library update can change defaults, and a table that is still being updated is not the same data.
Once these are pinned, the same inputs should give the same metric, or at least one within a known noise range.
r: Pin versions, seeds and data to reproduce a run.

q: The average latency of a model service is fine, but users complain about slow responses. What do you look at?
o: The average only: it is fine
The size of the training data
The accuracy of the model
Percentile latencies (p95, p99) broken down by stage: queueing, feature lookup, preprocessing and model
e:
The average hides the slow tail: a few percent of requests can be many times slower and still leave the mean looking good, while every user meets them sometimes.
Break the time down by stage. Typical culprits are cold starts, waiting in the batching queue, a slow feature lookup, garbage collection and noisy neighbours.
Set the service-level target on a percentile, such as p99 below 300 ms.
r: Averages hide the tail: use percentiles by stage.

q: A GPU-based model service has spiky traffic. Scaling on CPU usage reacts badly. What is a better signal for autoscaling?
o: The time of day
A signal that reflects the real load of this workload, such as requests in flight, queue length or latency
The number of developers online
The size of the model file
e:
For GPU inference the CPU is often not the bottleneck, so CPU usage can stay low while requests pile up.
Scaling on concurrency (requests in flight), queue length or latency follows the real pressure. Also account for the time a new replica needs to load the model, which can take minutes, and keep a margin or a minimum number of replicas.
Scaling to zero saves money but adds cold-start latency.
r: Scale on load signals that fit the workload.

q: What does quantizing a model do?
o: It trains the model on more data
It encrypts the model file
It adds layers to the model
It stores weights (and sometimes activations) in lower-precision numbers, such as 8-bit integers, to cut size and speed up inference, with a possible small loss of accuracy
e:
Weights are normally 32-bit floating-point numbers. Converting them to 8-bit integers or 16-bit floats makes the model smaller, uses less memory bandwidth and can run faster on suitable hardware.
Accuracy can drop a little, so measure it with your own evaluation set, on the target hardware, before shipping.
Pruning and distillation are related ways to get a smaller model.
r: Quantization: smaller and faster, check the accuracy.

q: An upstream team renames a column. The pipeline silently fills the feature with nulls, and model quality collapses weeks later. What would have caught it early?
o: Data validation checks at ingestion (schema, null rate, ranges, distributions) that fail the pipeline or raise an alert
A bigger model
More frequent retraining
A faster GPU
e:
Many ML failures are data failures that nobody sees, because the code keeps running. Retraining on the broken data would just make the model learn the breakage.
Validate the data at the pipeline's entrance and before training: expected columns and types, maximum share of nulls, value ranges, and distribution checks against a reference. Tools such as TFDV or Great Expectations help.
Fail fast and tell the owner of the data.
r: Validate data at the door; fail fast.

q: A pipeline step failed halfway and was run again, and now the training table has duplicated rows. Which design principle prevents this?
o: Never re-run failed steps
Add more workers
Make steps idempotent: running a step twice gives the same result, for example by overwriting a date partition instead of appending blindly
Store the table in a different format
e:
Failures and retries are normal in pipelines. If a step appends rows, a retry duplicates them.
An idempotent step writes its output so that repeating it replaces the same result: it overwrites a partition keyed by the run date, or it upserts by a unique key.
This also makes backfills (re-running past dates) safe.
r: Idempotent steps make retries and backfills safe.

q: What should continuous integration for an ML project run, in addition to unit tests?
o: Nothing else: unit tests are enough
Data and schema checks, a quick training run on a small sample, an evaluation gate against a baseline, and a test that the model can be packaged and served
A full training run on all the data for every commit
Only code formatting checks
e:
Code can pass its unit tests while the pipeline is broken. ML adds failure modes that CI can check cheaply.
A smoke training run on a small sample shows that the code runs end to end. A quality gate compares the model with a baseline or the current model. A serving test checks that the packaged model loads and answers.
Training on all the data for every commit is too slow and costly; save it for scheduled runs.
r: CI for ML tests code, data and model.

q: An auditor asks which data and code produced the model that was in production on 3 March. What do you need to have kept?
o: Only the final accuracy number
A screenshot of the dashboard
A registry entry linking each model version to its code commit, data snapshot, parameters, evaluation results, and the deployment history
The laptop of the data scientist
e:
Lineage is the traceable chain from the production model back to its sources. Without it, "which model was live on 3 March?" and "what was it trained on?" cannot be answered.
Keeping this record automatically in the pipeline and the registry is far more reliable than trying to rebuild it afterwards.
It also helps in incidents, to know which other models used the same data.
r: Keep lineage: model to code, data and parameters.

q: The same inputs reach a prediction service again and again, and each call is slow. What is a cheap way to speed it up?
o: Train a bigger model
Remove the monitoring
Disable logging
Cache predictions keyed by the input (and the model version), with an expiry time
e:
If inputs repeat, a cache returns the stored result in microseconds instead of running the model.
Put the model version in the cache key, so a new model never serves old answers, and set an expiry for data that changes. Only cache predictions that are deterministic and not personal in a way that would leak between users.
Measure the hit rate to see if it is worth it.
r: Cache by input + model version, with an expiry.

q: The online metric of a model slowly gets worse over several weeks. How do you investigate?
a:
- Confirm it is real: check the metric definition, the sample size and seasonality before blaming the model.
- Rule out the service and the data pipeline: errors, latency, missing or late data, changed schemas or units.
- Compare live inputs with the training reference (drift) and look at the prediction distribution, overall and by slice.
- Compare live features with the same features recomputed offline to look for training-serving skew.
- When labels are available, check whether the quality fell on all slices or only on some, and since when.
- Check what changed around that date: code, model version, upstream data, product or user behaviour.
- Then act: fix the data or the code, retrain with recent data through the normal gate, or roll back, and add a monitor so it is caught earlier next time.

q: A recommender is retrained every week on clicks. Over months the catalogue it shows gets narrower and narrower. What is happening?
o: Data leakage
A feedback loop: the model's own recommendations shape the clicks it is later trained on, so it reinforces what it already shows
Overfitting to the test set
A bug in the GPU
e:
The training data comes from users' reaction to what the previous model chose to show. Items it never shows get no clicks, so the next model has no reason to show them.
Ways to break the loop: keep some exploration (show random or uncertain items to a small share of users), log what was shown (impressions) and correct for the exposure bias, and measure diversity as well as clicks.
This kind of problem is invisible in offline metrics computed on the same logs.
r: Models that influence their own data need exploration.

q: What should an automated canary check before it increases the traffic share of a new model?
o: Health metrics (errors, latency, resource use), the distribution of predictions and the business metrics against the baseline, over a large enough sample, with thresholds that trigger a halt or a rollback
Only that the container starts
That nobody complained on chat
That the new model is larger than the old one
e:
A canary is useful only if it decides on evidence. Compare the new version with the baseline running at the same time on comparable traffic, so that time-of-day effects cancel.
Check the service (errors, latency), the model (prediction distribution, a sudden constant or shift) and the product (conversion or whichever metric matters), and define in advance the thresholds and the minimum sample size.
If a threshold is crossed, stop the ramp-up and roll back automatically.
r: Canary gates compare against the baseline with thresholds set in advance.

q: The team that owns the "active user" feature changes its definition, and your model's quality drops without any change on your side. What helps prevent this?
o: Data contracts and versioned features: agreed schemas and definitions, change notifications, and automatic validation of the incoming data
Hope it does not happen again
Retrain the model every hour
Stop using shared features
e:
Models depend on upstream data they do not control. A change of meaning keeps the same column name and type, so a schema check alone does not see it.
A data contract states what each field means, its type, ranges and freshness, who owns it and how changes are announced. Versioning lets the model keep reading v1 until it is retrained for v2, and validation alerts when the data stops matching the contract.
Treat upstream data like an API you consume.
r: Treat upstream data like an API: contract, version, validate.

q: An automatic weekly retraining job trained on data corrupted by an upstream bug, and the worse model went live. Which safeguard was missing?
o: A larger training set
A faster training cluster
A promotion gate: evaluate the candidate against the current model on a fixed, trusted holdout and on data-quality checks, and only promote it if it passes, with a quick rollback
More frequent retraining
e:
Automation without a gate turns any data problem into a production problem. A new model should have to earn its place.
The gate compares the candidate with the current champion on a fixed evaluation set that does not change with the new data, checks for regressions on important slices, and runs the data validation on the training set. A failed gate keeps the old model and alerts a person.
The old version stays deployable for a rollback.
r: Retraining needs a promotion gate.

q: A fraud model needs the feature "number of transactions by this card in the last 5 minutes", but features are computed in a daily batch job. Why is this not enough?
o: The batch job is too fast
The feature would be up to a day old and would miss the burst of activity the model is meant to detect; it needs fresh values computed from a stream, using the same logic as in training
The model cannot use counts
Batch jobs cannot be scheduled
e:
Feature freshness must match the decision. A feature that is hours old cannot describe what happened five minutes ago, and the signal is lost.
Compute such windowed features from a stream (or on demand from recent events) and serve them from an online store. The same definition must also produce the training values, with point-in-time correctness, or you get training-serving skew.
Slow-moving features (customer age, account type) can stay in batch.
r: Feature freshness must match the decision's timescale.

q: Overall model quality is stable, but support tickets show it works badly for customers in one region. Which monitoring practice would have shown this?
o: Looking only at the overall average
Counting the number of requests
Checking uptime
Computing quality and data metrics by slice (region, device, customer type) and alerting on each slice
e:
An average can be stable while a small group gets much worse results, because the large groups hide it.
Monitor important slices separately for data drift, prediction distribution and quality metrics, with enough volume to be meaningful. The same slices belong in the evaluation gate before a release.
Pick the slices from business risk and from where the data differs, since you cannot alert on all combinations.
r: Monitor by slice, not only overall.

q: Design how you would deploy and monitor a fraud scoring model that must answer in under 100 ms.
a:
- Serving: an online API behind a container, with the model quantized or sized to meet the latency target, and the p95 and p99 latencies tracked by stage.
- Features: a feature store with an online part for fresh, windowed features and an offline part for training, from the same definitions and with point-in-time joins.
- Release: shadow first, then a small canary against the current model with automatic halt thresholds, and an instant rollback to the previous version in the registry.
- Monitoring: service health, input and prediction distributions by slice, and fraud labels as they arrive (often days later), with alerts on size of change.
- Retraining: on a schedule plus drift triggers, with data validation and a promotion gate on a fixed holdout that includes the recent period.
- Safety nets: a fallback rule-based score if the model or the feature store fails, caching where useful, and an audit trail of model version, features and decision for each score.
- Feedback: investigators' decisions go back as labels, taking care of selection bias, because only flagged cases get reviewed.

q: How do you decide between batch, online and streaming inference for a new use case?
a:
- Latency need: if nobody waits for the result, use batch; if a user or system waits for seconds or milliseconds, use online.
- Freshness of the inputs: if the decision depends on events from the last minutes, you need streaming features, whatever the serving mode.
- Volume and cost: batch uses hardware efficiently and is cheap; online needs always-on capacity, autoscaling and headroom for peaks.
- Reuse: precomputing predictions for a limited set of entities (users, products) in batch and serving them from a store is often the simplest option that is fast enough.
- Complexity and operations: each step towards real time adds monitoring, on-call and consistency work between training and serving.
- Failure plan: what happens if the model is unavailable? A stale batch result or a rule-based default can be a good fallback.
- Start with the simplest mode that meets the requirement, and move to a more complex one only when the numbers justify it.
